plan.english: Let your blood grow with blood.

cognate_refs.locus: KUB 9.4 i 17–18 (+ KUB 55.20; CTH 760 per West 2007 ch. 8 n. 68, filed under CTH 409 in TLH)

notes: The 'blood to blood' polyptoton with the same heteroclitic noun in both branches: AV ásṛk ... asnā́ (nom. + instr.), Hittite ešḫar=kan ešḫani ḫandan 'blood is fitted to blood' (nom. + dat.-loc.), in the list bone-sinew-blood that Watkins (1995: 529) and West (2007 ch. 8) compare with Merseburg II bluot zi bluoda (OHG bluot is not cognate). Instrumental follows the Vedic. The verb is interpolated: h₁léwdʰeti continues Vedic rohatu (ruh- < *h₁lewdʰ- 'grow'); Hittite has ḫandai- 'fit'. The enclitic 'your' (Ved. te) is interpolated.

plan.english: Set marrow with marrow; let your blood grow with blood.

cognate_refs.locus: Contra vermes (Munich ms., Braune–Helm Ahd. Lesebuch no. 89)
KUB 9.4 i 17–18 (+ KUB 55.20; CTH 760 per West 2007 ch. 8 n. 68, filed under CTH 409 in TLH)

notes: Two adjacent pādas of AV 4.12.4. Marrow *mosgʰo- is Watkins's key word of the inherited list of the body's constituents (1995: 523–34): Ved. majján-, OHG/Old Saxon marg in the nesso worm charm, Danish-Norwegian 'marv i marv' in a late Merseburg-type spell (Kuhn); only the OHG charm is cited as a ref. Blood as in healing-charms-001. Vedic has the n-stem majján-; the thematic *mosgʰó- of Germanic, Avestan and Slavic is the lexeme used. The active imperative 'set!' of dʰeh₁ follows chinnáṃ sáṃ dhehi 'set together what is severed (o herb)' of 4.12.7, since the engine has no 3sg middle imperative for sáṃ dhīyatām (Vedic only, interpolated); sám 'together' has no usable lexeme and is left out.

Watkins's proto-text of the IE charm (1995: 534): the slaying verb *gʷʰen- linked by contiguity with the list ending in MARROW (*mosgʰo-) in India (AV 12.5.70 majjñó asya nír jahi), Germanic (nesso charm: worm driven out from the marrow) and Ireland (gono mil 'I slay the beast'). Vedic jahi is the 2sg imperative of the athematic present (gʷʰénti). 'Out' is interpolated with úd (Ved. nír has no usable etymon); 'his' with the demonstrative (Ved. asya).

The worm charm's paean in the 1st singular present: AV vaḥ krimayo hanmi 'I slay you, o worms' and Old Irish gono mil 'I slay the beast' (the only attestation of the 1sg absolute of gonaid), 'two performances of the same text' (Watkins 1995: 520–2; West 2007 ch. 8). Both are the athematic 1sg *gʷʰénmi. The objects are not cognate (kṛ́mi- 'worm' vs mil 'beast' ~ Gk μῆλον), and neither 'worm' nor *meh₁lo- is a usable lexeme, so only the Vedic enclitic 'you (pl.)' is kept, interpolated.

The words that close a successful cure: AV 4.12.7 práti tiṣṭhordhváḥ 'stand firm upright', said to the healed patient, and Pindar's Asclepius who set his patients on their feet, ἔστασεν ὀρθούς, after incantation, drugs and surgery (West 2007 ch. 8). Same root *steh₂- and same adjective *h₃r̥dʰwó- in both; Vedic has the reduplicated present imperative, Greek the transitive s-aorist; the root-aorist imperative is the lexicon's form. próti (Ved. práti) is Vedic only, interpolated.
